claim: When epithelia become too crowded, some cells are extruded that later die.
source: When epithelia become too crowded, some cells are extruded that later die.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rosenblatt et al., 2001; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: To extrude, a cell produces the lipid, Sphingosine 1-Phosphate (S1P), which activates S1P2 receptors in neighboring cells that seamlessly squeeze the cell out of the epithelium.
source: To extrude, a cell produces the lipid, Sphingosine 1-Phosphate (S1P), which activates S1P2 receptors in neighboring cells that seamlessly squeeze the cell out of the epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by prior research (Gu et al., 2011) establishing the S1P-S1P2 signaling mechanism.

claim: Tumors or epithelia lacking S1P2 cannot extrude cells apically.
source: Tumors or epithelia lacking S1P2 cannot extrude cells apically and instead form apoptotic-resistant masses, possess poor barrier function, and shift extrusion basally beneath the epithelium, providing a potential mechanism for cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 4, and 5 demonstrating extrusion defects in S1P2-deficient cells.

claim: Epithelia lacking S1P2 form apoptotic-resistant masses.
source: Tumors or epithelia lacking S1P2 cannot extrude cells apically and instead form apoptotic-resistant masses, possess poor barrier function, and shift extrusion basally beneath the epithelium, providing a potential mechanism for cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1B, 1D, 1E, and 4C showing mass formation in S1P2-depleted cells.

claim: Epithelia lacking S1P2 possess poor barrier function.
source: Tumors or epithelia lacking S1P2 cannot extrude cells apically and instead form apoptotic-resistant masses, possess poor barrier function, and shift extrusion basally beneath the epithelium, providing a potential mechanism for cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A showing increased Texas Red-Dextran permeability in S1P2 mutant zebrafish.

claim: Epithelia lacking S1P2 shift extrusion basally beneath the epithelium.
source: Tumors or epithelia lacking S1P2 cannot extrude cells apically and instead form apoptotic-resistant masses, possess poor barrier function, and shift extrusion basally beneath the epithelium, providing a potential mechanism for cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4D, 4E, and 5C showing increased basal extrusion in S1P2-deficient cells.

claim: Exogenous S1P2 expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion.
source: Exogenous S1P2 expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion, cell death, and reduce orthotopic pancreatic tumors and their metastases.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing that S1P2-GFP expression rescues apical extrusion in HPAF II cells.

claim: Exogenous S1P2 expression is sufficient to rescue cell death.
source: Exogenous S1P2 expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion, cell death, and reduce orthotopic pancreatic tumors and their metastases.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5E showing increased dying cells in lumens of HPAF II-S1P2 cysts.

claim: Exogenous S1P2 expression reduces orthotopic pancreatic tumors and their metastases.
source: Exogenous S1P2 expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion, cell death, and reduce orthotopic pancreatic tumors and their metastases.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8 showing reduced tumor weight and metastatic frequency in HPAF II-S1P2 tumors.

claim: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitor can bypass extrusion defects.
source: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitor can bypass extrusion defects and could, therefore, target pancreatic, lung, and colon tumors that lack S1P2 without affecting wild-type tissue.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D showing that FAK inhibitor rescues apoptosis in extrusion-deficient cells.

claim: FAK inhibitor could target pancreatic, lung, and colon tumors that lack S1P2 without affecting wild-type tissue.
source: Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) inhibitor can bypass extrusion defects and could, therefore, target pancreatic, lung, and colon tumors that lack S1P2 without affecting wild-type tissue.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 showing FAK inhibitor eliminates masses in S1P2 mutant zebrafish without affecting wild-type fish, and by inference from the selective effect on extrusion-deficient cells.

claim: The stretch-activated channel Piezo-1 senses cell crowding and enables some cells to produce S1P.
source: The stretch-activated channel Piezo-1 senses cell crowding and enables some cells to produce the bioactive sphingolipid, Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), which binds G-protein coupled receptors (S1P2) in neighboring cells to activate Rho-mediated assembly and contraction of an intercellular actomyosin ring (Gu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gu et al., 2011) establishing the Piezo-1 mechanism.

claim: S1P binds G-protein coupled receptors (S1P2) in neighboring cells to activate Rho-mediated assembly and contraction of an intercellular actomyosin ring.
source: The stretch-activated channel Piezo-1 senses cell crowding and enables some cells to produce the bioactive sphingolipid, Sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), which binds G-protein coupled receptors (S1P2) in neighboring cells to activate Rho-mediated assembly and contraction of an intercellular actomyosin ring (Gu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gu et al., 2011) establishing the S1P2-Rho signaling mechanism.

claim: Actomyosin ring contraction squeezes live cells apically out of the epithelial sheet while simultaneously closing the gap.
source: This contraction squeezes live cells apically out of the epithelial sheet while simultaneously closing the gap that might have resulted from the cell's exit, thus preserving epithelial barrier function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the extrusion mechanism and prior citations.

claim: Extrusion preserves epithelial barrier function.
source: This contraction squeezes live cells apically out of the epithelial sheet while simultaneously closing the gap that might have resulted from the cell's exit, thus preserving epithelial barrier function.
evidence: This is supported by inference from the mechanism and data in Figure 7A showing poor barrier function when extrusion is defective.

claim: Live extruded cells become stripped from the underlying matrix and its associated survival signaling, and later die by anoikis.
source: Because live extruded cells become stripped from the underlying matrix and its associated survival signaling, they later die by anoikis (Frisch and Francis, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Frisch and Francis, 1994) on anoikis.

claim: Advanced tumors typically have increased survival signaling that overrides anoikis.
source: Advanced tumors typically have increased survival signaling that overrides anoikis, suggesting that cells could survive following extrusion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about tumor cell survival mechanisms.

claim: Epithelia typically extrude cells apically into the lumen of the tissue.
source: Typically, epithelia extrude cells apically into the lumen of the tissue (Slattum et al., 2009), which would act to essentially eliminate tumor cells with upregulated survival signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Slattum et al., 2009).

claim: Some cells are extruded basally into the tissue encased by the epithelium.
source: However, some cells are extruded basally into the tissue encased by the epithelium (Slattum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Slattum et al., 2009).

claim: Basally extruded cells that survive following extrusion might be able to invade into the underlying tissue.
source: If basally extruded cells survive following extrusion, they might be able to invade into the underlying tissue (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to prior work (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014).

claim: Oncogenic mutations in adenomatous polyposis coli or K-Ras misregulate apical extrusion and drive extrusion basally.
source: Interestingly, we have found that oncogenic mutations in either adenomatous polyposis coli or K-Ras misregulate apical extrusion and drive extrusion basally (Marshall et al., 2011; Slattum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Marshall et al., 2011; Slattum et al., 2014).

claim: S1P2-depleted HBE epithelia accumulated into masses over three layers thick whereas control-knockdown monolayers retained a single layer.
source: S1P2-depleted HBE epithelia, which are extrusion-deficient (Gu et al., 2011), accumulated into masses over three layers thick whereas control-knockdown monolayers retained a single layer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: S1P2 depletion did not affect the proliferation rate in HBE cells.
source: Because cell extrusion typically promotes epithelial cell death (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012) and because S1P2 depletion did not affect the proliferation rate in a yellow tetrazolium MTT (3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazolyl-2)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) assay (Figure 1C), masses were likely to arise due to reduced apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Masses in S1P2-depleted epithelia likely arise due to reduced apoptosis.
source: Because cell extrusion typically promotes epithelial cell death (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012) and because S1P2 depletion did not affect the proliferation rate in a yellow tetrazolium MTT (3-(4, 5-dimethylthiazolyl-2)-2, 5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) assay (Figure 1C), masses were likely to arise due to reduced apoptosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of unchanged proliferation and mass formation, supported by citations (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012).

claim: Zebrafish larvae carrying a loss-of-function mutation in S1P2 (Miles apart [Mil]) cannot extrude apoptotic epidermal cells.
source: Additionally, zebrafish larvae carrying a loss-of-function mutation in S1P2 (Miles apart [Mil]) cannot extrude apoptotic epidermal cells (Gu et al., 2011), and similarly accumulated numerous epidermal cell aggregates throughout the body (18 ± 3.5 aggregates/fish, n = 22) by only 5 days post fertilization (dpf) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gu et al., 2011) and data in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Mil zebrafish mutants accumulated numerous epidermal cell aggregates throughout the body (18 ± 3.5 aggregates/fish, n = 22) by 5 days post fertilization.
source: Additionally, zebrafish larvae carrying a loss-of-function mutation in S1P2 (Miles apart [Mil]) cannot extrude apoptotic epidermal cells (Gu et al., 2011), and similarly accumulated numerous epidermal cell aggregates throughout the body (18 ± 3.5 aggregates/fish, n = 22) by only 5 days post fertilization (dpf) (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Masses were undetectable in heterozygote Mil or WT siblings of the same age.
source: By contrast, masses were undetectable in heterozygote Mil or WT siblings of the same age (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: HBE monolayers lacking S1P2 had greatly reduced rates of apoptosis in response to UV-C compared to controls.
source: HBE monolayers lacking S1P2 (Figure 2A) or treated with a selective S1P2 receptor antagonist, JTE-013 (Figure 2B) had greatly reduced rates of apoptosis in response to a strong apoptotic stimulus, UV-C, compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: HBE monolayers treated with S1P2 receptor antagonist JTE-013 had greatly reduced rates of apoptosis in response to UV-C compared to controls.
source: HBE monolayers lacking S1P2 (Figure 2A) or treated with a selective S1P2 receptor antagonist, JTE-013 (Figure 2B) had greatly reduced rates of apoptosis in response to a strong apoptotic stimulus, UV-C, compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MDCK monolayers treated with S1P2 antagonist were resistant to several common chemotherapy drugs that cause apoptosis.
source: Madin–Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) monolayers treated with S1P2 antagonist were similarly resistant to several common chemotherapy drugs that cause apoptosis (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The reduced cell death rates in epithelia lacking S1P2 were due to disruption of extrusion rather than altered S1P signaling.
source: The reduced cell death rates in epithelia lacking S1P2 were due to disruption of extrusion rather than altered S1P signaling, since other inhibitors of extrusion, Rho kinase inhibitor (Y-27632), myosin II inhibitor (Blebbistatin), or Rac inhibitor (EHT1864) all decreased cell death rates to the extent that they inhibit extrusion (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating that multiple extrusion inhibitors reduce cell death.

claim: The ratio of cell death to extrusion inhibition is approximately 1:1 for various extrusion inhibitors.
source: In each case, the ratio of cell death to extrusion inhibition is ∼1:1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Inhibition of apoptosis was not due to increasing levels of S1P.
source: Inhibition of apoptosis was not due to increasing levels of S1P, which can act as a pro-survival signal, as S1P levels in apoptotic cells varied independently of extrusion inhibition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B demonstrating that S1P levels do not correlate with extrusion inhibition.

claim: Inhibitors that blocked apoptosis by blocking extrusion in an intact monolayer do not impact the apoptosis rates of single cells that are incapable of extrusion.
source: Since freshly plated single MDCK cells are resistant to apoptotic stimuli, we tested if these same compounds reduced apoptosis in similarly aged single MDCKs by treating with EGTA to disrupt cadherin-dependent cell–cell contacts. Inhibitors that blocked apoptosis by blocking extrusion in an intact monolayer do not impact the apoptosis rates of single cells that are incapable of extrusion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: UV-induced apoptosis was unaltered in single HBE cells lacking S1P2 when HBE monolayers were treated with EGTA.
source: Similarly, UV-induced apoptosis was unaltered in single HBE cells lacking S1P2 when HBE monolayers where treated with EGTA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Inhibiting S1P2 with JTE-013 in NIH 3T3 fibroblasts does not affect the cell death rate in response to UV-C.
source: Additionally, inhibiting S1P2 with JTE-013 in a cell line that cannot extrude but expresses this receptor (Clair et al., 2003; Pham et al., 2013), NIH 3T3 fibroblasts, does not affect the cell death rate in response to UV-C (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and citations (Clair et al., 2003; Pham et al., 2013).

claim: Increased cell survival is linked with the inability to extrude rather than to any intrinsic block of the apoptosis pathway.
source: These data together suggest that increased cell survival is linked with the inability to extrude rather than to any intrinsic block of the apoptosis pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that extrusion inhibitors do not affect apoptosis in single cells.

claim: S1P2 mRNA is significantly reduced in PDAC compared to normal tissues.
source: Our analysis of published tumor microarray data found S1P2 mRNA to be significantly reduced in PDAC (Buchholz et al., 2005; Segara et al., 2005; Badea et al., 2008), and some lung and colon tumors (Bhattacharjee et al., 2001), compared to their corresponding normal tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published tumor microarray data (Buchholz et al., 2005; Segara et al., 2005; Badea et al., 2008).

claim: S1P2 mRNA is significantly reduced in some lung and colon tumors compared to normal tissues.
source: Our analysis of published tumor microarray data found S1P2 mRNA to be significantly reduced in PDAC (Buchholz et al., 2005; Segara et al., 2005; Badea et al., 2008), and some lung and colon tumors (Bhattacharjee et al., 2001), compared to their corresponding normal tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published tumor microarray data (Bhattacharjee et al., 2001).

claim: HPAF II pancreatic adenocarcinoma cells have reduced S1P2 levels.
source: To investigate if cancer cells lacking S1P2 also have extrusion and apoptosis defects, we analyzed a pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell line, HPAF II, that has reduced S1P2 levels (Figure 4A) and forms epithelial monolayers necessary for assaying extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HPAF II cells formed masses within a week of culture.
source: Similar to HBE monolayers lacking S1P2, HPAF II cells formed masses within a week of culture and displayed extrusion defects and reduced rates of UV-C-induce apoptosis (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A-D.

claim: HPAF II cells displayed extrusion defects and reduced rates of UV-C-induced apoptosis.
source: Similar to HBE monolayers lacking S1P2, HPAF II cells formed masses within a week of culture and displayed extrusion defects and reduced rates of UV-C-induce apoptosis (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A-D.

claim: Approximately 50% of HPAF II cells did not extrude, and most of the remaining cells extruded basally.
source: While ∼50% of cells did not extrude, most of the remaining cells extruded in the opposite direction—basally, underneath the layer (Figure 4D,E) at rates similar to when MDCK monolayers are treated with S1P2 antagonist (Slattum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E, and citation (Slattum et al., 2014).

claim: Approximately 30% of HPAF II cysts extrude cells basally that survive, compared to only approximately 3% of MDCK cysts.
source: Approximately 30% of HPAF II cysts extrude cells basally that survive, compared to only ∼3% of MDCK cysts (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: 28.6% of basally extruded HPAF II cells remained alive throughout a 12-hr video, whereas those from MDCK cysts died during this time.
source: Live imaging confirmed that 28.6% of basally extruded cells remained alive throughout a 12-hr video, whereas those from MDCK cysts died during this time (Video 1, n = 5 videos of each).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 1.

claim: S1P2-GFP expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion in HPAF II cells.
source: Importantly, S1P2-GFP expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion (Figure 5C), decrease the frequency of live cells that basally extrude (Figure 5D), and increase the percentage of cysts with dead cells in their lumens (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: S1P2-GFP expression decreases the frequency of live cells that basally extrude in HPAF II cysts.
source: Importantly, S1P2-GFP expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion (Figure 5C), decrease the frequency of live cells that basally extrude (Figure 5D), and increase the percentage of cysts with dead cells in their lumens (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: S1P2-GFP expression increases the percentage of cysts with dead cells in their lumens in HPAF II cysts.
source: Importantly, S1P2-GFP expression is sufficient to rescue apical extrusion (Figure 5C), decrease the frequency of live cells that basally extrude (Figure 5D), and increase the percentage of cysts with dead cells in their lumens (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The S1P-S1P2 signaling required for extrusion is critical for promoting cell death and for preventing basal extrusion.
source: These data suggest that the S1P-S1P2 signaling required for extrusion is critical not only for promoting cell death but also for preventing basal extrusion, which could enable cells to invade.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue of apical extrusion and cell death by S1P2 expression.

claim: Control MDCK cells in early stages of extrusion have far higher levels of active FAK than surrounding live cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that control MDCK cells in early stages of extrusion have far higher levels of active FAK, by immunostaining with a phospho-FAK antibody, than surrounding live cells but that these levels decrease during later stages of extrusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Active FAK levels decrease during later stages of extrusion in control MDCK cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that control MDCK cells in early stages of extrusion have far higher levels of active FAK, by immunostaining with a phospho-FAK antibody, than surrounding live cells but that these levels decrease during later stages of extrusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Late-staged apoptotic cells still have high levels of active FAK when extrusion is blocked with S1P2 antagonist.
source: However, late-staged apoptotic cells (detected by piknotic DNA) still have high levels of active FAK when extrusion is blocked with S1P2 antagonist (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The specific FAK inhibitor PF 573228 had no effect on untreated or UV-treated wild type monolayers.
source: The specific FAK inhibitor PF 573228 had no effect on untreated or UV-treated wild type monolayers (Figure 6B and [Slack-Davis et al., 2007]), likely because cells not targeted to extrude have quite low levels of active FAK (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and citation (Slack-Davis et al., 2007).

claim: FAK inhibitor rescued the cell death rates of monolayers where extrusion is blocked with S1P2 antagonist or Rac inhibitor to those seen in wild type monolayers.
source: However, this same FAK inhibitor rescued the cell death rates of monolayers where extrusion is blocked with S1P2 antagonist JTE013 or Rac inhibitor to those seen in wild type monolayers (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Over-expression of a dominant negative FAK isoform (FRNK) acted similarly to FAK inhibitor.
source: Over-expression of a dominant negative FAK isoform (FRNK) (Park et al., 2004) acted similarly to FAK inhibitor (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and citation (Park et al., 2004).

claim: FAK inhibitor alone induced apoptosis of HPAF II cells in monolayers.
source: Importantly, FAK inhibitor alone induced apoptosis of HPAF II cells in monolayers (Figure 6D) and even those basally extruding from HPAF II cysts (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: FAK inhibitor induced apoptosis of HPAF II cells basally extruding from cysts.
source: Importantly, FAK inhibitor alone induced apoptosis of HPAF II cells in monolayers (Figure 6D) and even those basally extruding from HPAF II cysts (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: Treatment with FAK inhibitor to cysts that had already accumulated live basally extruded cells was sufficient to nearly double apoptosis rates of basally extruded cells (from 15 ± 2% to 28 ± 3%) when added for only 2 hr.
source: Additionally, treatment with FAK inhibitor to cysts that had already accumulated live basally extruded cells was sufficient to nearly double apoptosis rates of basally extruded cells (from 15 ± 2% to 28 ± 3%) when added for only 2 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: FAK inhibitor had no visible effect on wild-type zebrafish at 5 dpf.
source: While FAK inhibitor had no visible effect on wild-type zebrafish at 5 dpf, it greatly decreased the number and size of epidermal cell masses in S1P2-mutant embryos of the same age (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: FAK inhibitor greatly decreased the number and size of epidermal cell masses in S1P2-mutant zebrafish embryos at 5 dpf.
source: While FAK inhibitor had no visible effect on wild-type zebrafish at 5 dpf, it greatly decreased the number and size of epidermal cell masses in S1P2-mutant embryos of the same age (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: FAK inhibitor treatment sloughed off many of the epidermal cells and increased the apoptosis rate within the masses.
source: While FAK inhibitor treatment sloughed off many of the epidermal cells, which could be found at the bottom of the dish, it also increased the apoptosis rate within the masses (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: S1P2 morphants had 0.18-fold lower S1P2 protein levels.
source: S1P2 morphants had 0.18-fold lower S1P2 protein levels (Figure 7E) and phenocopied the epidermal masses seen in Mil mutants (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: S1P2 morphants phenocopied the epidermal masses seen in Mil mutants.
source: S1P2 morphants had 0.18-fold lower S1P2 protein levels (Figure 7E) and phenocopied the epidermal masses seen in Mil mutants (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Addition of FAK inhibitor to an S1P2 morphant at 5 dpf with epidermal masses caused the masses to slough off within 19 hr.
source: Addition of FAK inhibitor to an S1P2 morphant at 5 dpf with epidermal masses caused the masses to slough off within 19 hr (Figure 7F, where n = 6 videos total).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Mil embryos had poor epidermal barrier function, as assayed by Texas Red-DextranMW70 permeability.
source: Remarkably, we found that while Mil embryos had poor epidermal barrier function, as assayed by Texas Red-DextranMW70 permeability, epidermal permeability was significantly reduced with FAK inhibitor (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Epidermal permeability was significantly reduced with FAK inhibitor in Mil embryos.
source: Remarkably, we found that while Mil embryos had poor epidermal barrier function, as assayed by Texas Red-DextranMW70 permeability, epidermal permeability was significantly reduced with FAK inhibitor (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: S1P2 expression was sufficient to markedly reduce both tumor size and metastatic frequency in orthotopic HPAF II tumors.
source: To test the role of S1P2 in tumorigenesis, we orthotopically transplanted HPAF II tumor cells expressing either GFP or S1P2-GFP into nude mice and found that S1P2 expression was sufficient to markedly reduce both tumor size and metastatic frequency (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: Human pancreatic carcinomas have strikingly down-regulated S1P2 protein levels.
source: Further, we found that human pancreatic carcinomas have strikingly down-regulated S1P2 protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: S1P2 was significantly lower in pancreatic cancer (PDAC) cells compared to epithelial acini from uninvolved neck margins or to pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) precursor lesions.
source: We found that S1P2 was significantly lower in pancreatic cancer (PDAC) cells compared to epithelial acini from uninvolved neck margins, from which PDACs may arise, or to pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) precursor lesions (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9A-C.

claim: Lower S1P2 expression correlates with later tumor stages in both averaged and five patient-matched samples.
source: Importantly, lower S1P2 expression correlates with later tumor stages in both averaged (Figure 9B) and five patient-matched samples (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9B and 9C.

claim: Loss of S1P2 expression in pancreatic cancers suggests that defective extrusion may contribute to human PDAC development.
source: Loss of S1P2 expression in pancreatic cancers suggests that defective extrusion may contribute to human PDAC development.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between S1P2 loss and tumor progression.

claim: Normal epithelial cells produce S1P to trigger their extrusion and death once they become too crowded, simultaneously maintaining correct cell density and barrier function.
source: Normal epithelial cells produce S1P to trigger their extrusion and death once they become too crowded, simultaneously maintaining correct cell density and barrier function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior work and the current study.

claim: Epithelia with defective S1P/S1P2 signaling cannot extrude apically.
source: Epithelia with defective S1P/S1P2 signaling cannot extrude apically.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Extrusion-defective epithelia retain cells, which can result in resistance to homeostatic and chemotherapy-induced cell death and neoplastic masses.
source: Extrusion-defective epithelia retain cells, which can result in resistance to homeostatic and chemotherapy-induced cell death and neoplastic masses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: A small number of cells also die without getting extruded, which can disrupt barrier function.
source: Further, a small number of cells also die without getting extruded, which can disrupt barrier function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating poor barrier function.

claim: Poor epithelia barrier function could cause chronic inflammation—an important factor for tumor progression.
source: Aside from allowing access of inappropriate signals, poor epithelia barrier function could cause chronic inflammation—an important factor for tumor progression (Coussens and Werb, 2002).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation (Coussens and Werb, 2002).

claim: Defective apical extrusion signaling shifts extrusion basally, which could allow transformed cells to invade the underlying tissue.
source: Additionally, defective apical extrusion signaling shifts extrusion basally, which could allow transformed cells to invade the underlying tissue (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014).

claim: Oncogenic KRasV12 expression degrades S1P through autophagy and causes cell masses and basal extrusion.
source: We have recently discovered that oncogenic KRasV12 expression degrades S1P through autophagy and causes cell masses and basal extrusion, similar to the extrusion defects observed when S1P2 is absent (Slattum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work (Slattum et al., 2014).

claim: KRasV12 is an important driver for pancreatic, lung, and colon carcinomas.
source: KRasV12 is an important driver for the same cancers that lack S1P2—pancreatic, lung, and colon carcinomas—and its expression alone reduces S1P2 (Slattum et al., 2014), which may explain why PanIN precursors have reduced S1P2 expression.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and citation (Slattum et al., 2014).

claim: KRasV12 expression alone reduces S1P2.
source: KRasV12 is an important driver for the same cancers that lack S1P2—pancreatic, lung, and colon carcinomas—and its expression alone reduces S1P2 (Slattum et al., 2014), which may explain why PanIN precursors have reduced S1P2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation (Slattum et al., 2014).

claim: Truncation of the adenomatous polyposis coli gene results in increased basal extrusion.
source: Further, we have found that another oncogenic mutation, truncation of the adenomatous polyposis coli gene, also results in increased basal extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by prior findings from the authors' work.

claim: Exogenous expression of S1P2 can dramatically reduce basal extrusion rates and orthotopic tumor metastasis rates in tumor cells that lack this receptor.
source: While it is not clear what mechanisms drive tumor cell invasion, our work showing that exogenous expression of S1P2 can dramatically reduce basal extrusion rates and orthotopic tumor metastasis rates in tumor cells that lack this receptor suggests that S1P2-mediated extrusion may play an important role in metastatic cell invasion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 8.

claim: S1P2-mediated extrusion may play an important role in metastatic cell invasion.
source: While it is not clear what mechanisms drive tumor cell invasion, our work showing that exogenous expression of S1P2 can dramatically reduce basal extrusion rates and orthotopic tumor metastasis rates in tumor cells that lack this receptor suggests that S1P2-mediated extrusion may play an important role in metastatic cell invasion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue of basal extrusion and metastasis by S1P2 expression.

claim: Cancer cells lacking S1P2 have increased survival signaling due to an inability to detach from the matrix and its associated survival signaling through increased active FAK.
source: Because cancer cells lacking S1P2 have increased survival signaling due to an inability to detach from the matrix and its associated survival signaling through increased active FAK, we found that FAK inhibitor on its own could rescue cell death rates to those seen in wild type cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating increased phospho-FAK in extrusion-blocked cells.

claim: FAK inhibitor could reverse extrusion defects such as poor barrier function and survival of basally extruded cells.
source: Surprisingly, FAK inhibitor could also reverse other extrusion defects, such as poor barrier function and survival of basally extruded cells, factors that together could contribute to tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Adding FAK inhibitor can rescue extrusion defects when added after they form.
source: The fact that adding FAK inhibitor can rescue these defects when added after they form further supports the notion that anoikis results from extrusion and also suggests that FAK inhibitors may be particularly good at treating pancreatic and other carcinomas defective in extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FAK inhibitor can eliminate pre-existing masses and basally extruded cells.

claim: A specific FAK inhibitor is not expected to cause the common toxicities associated with standard chemotherapies, as it does not affect normal epithelial tissue.
source: Moreover, we expect a specific FAK inhibitor to not cause the common toxicities associated with standard chemotherapies, as it does not affect normal epithelial tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental data showing FAK inhibitor does not affect wild-type zebrafish or normal monolayers.

claim: Another FAK inhibitor, PF-00562271, reduces tumor growth, metastases, and ameliorates tumor microenvironment when used in an orthotopic mouse model for pancreatic cancer.
source: Another FAK inhibitor, PF-00562271, reduces tumor growth, metastases, and ameliorates tumor microenvironment when used in an orthotopic mouse model for pancreatic cancer (Stokes et al., 2011), suggesting this drug could be promising for pancreatic cancer patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Stokes et al., 2011).

claim: PF-00562271 also inhibits a FAK-related kinase Pyk-2, which promotes non-specific cell death.
source: However, it is important to note that PF-00562271 also inhibits a FAK-related kinase Pyk-2, which promotes non-specific cell death (Schultze and Fiedler, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Schultze and Fiedler, 2011).

claim: The phase I clinical trial for PF-00562271 showed that while this drug was tolerated fairly well, it did cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
source: The phase I clinical trial for PF-00562271 showed that while this drug was tolerated fairly well, it did cause nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (Infante et al., 2012), symptoms indicative of poor gut barrier function, likely due to excessive non-specific apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical trial data (Infante et al., 2012).

claim: A newer more specific FAK inhibitor, such as VS-4718, may provide a more targeted therapy for patients with pancreatic and lung carcinomas that have aberrant extrusion signaling without the common toxicities associated with older chemotherapies.
source: Our results suggest that a newer more specific FAK inhibitor, such as VS-4718 (Shapiro et al., 2014), may provide a more targeted therapy for patients with pancreatic and lung carcinomas that have aberrant extrusion signaling without the common toxicities associated with older chemotherapies.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the study's findings and citation (Shapiro et al., 2014).

claim: Disruption of extrusion may contribute to a class of cancers with poor prognosis.
source: Based on our previous findings that extrusion drives normal epithelial cell turnover, we have found that disruption of extrusion may contribute to a class of cancers with poor prognosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cancer cells that lack the extrusion-signaling axis have reduced cell death rates, poor barrier function, and a propensity to extrude cells basally.
source: We find that cancer cells that lack the extrusion-signaling axis not only have reduced cell death rates but also have poor barrier function and a propensity to extrude cells basally, properties that could lead to higher invasion and metastatic rates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aberrant extrusion signaling in pancreatic and lung carcinomas could contribute to both tumor initiation and progression.
source: Therefore, aberrant extrusion signaling in pancreatic and lung carcinomas could not only contribute to tumor initiation but also progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing multiple tumor-promoting effects of defective extrusion.

claim: Specific inhibition of FAK does not disrupt normal epithelial tissue.
source: Importantly, specific inhibition of FAK, which does not disrupt normal epithelial tissue, is sufficient to reverse all of the effects of disrupted extrusion and could provide a better, less toxic therapy for this aggressive class of tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing FAK inhibitor does not affect wild-type cells.

claim: Specific inhibition of FAK is sufficient to reverse all of the effects of disrupted extrusion.
source: Importantly, specific inhibition of FAK, which does not disrupt normal epithelial tissue, is sufficient to reverse all of the effects of disrupted extrusion and could provide a better, less toxic therapy for this aggressive class of tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Mil zebrafish mutants die due to heart defects around 5 dpf.
source: To test if FAK inhibitor could eliminate epidermal masses after they form, we needed to inducibly knockdown S1P2 later in development, since Mil zebrafish mutants die due to heart defects around the time cell masses form (∼5 dpf; [Kupperman et al., 2000]).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Kupperman et al., 2000).

claim: MDCK cells form cysts with hollow apical lumens of 34 µm ± 5 µm in diameter when grown in Matrigel.
source: MDCKs were used as controls, which, like HPAF II cells, form cysts with hollow apical lumens of 34 µm ± 5 µm in diameter when grown in Matrigel (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Extrusion promotes cell death in response to apoptotic stimuli.
source: Because extrusion promotes cell death in response to apoptotic stimuli (Rosenblatt et al., 2001; Andrade and Rosenblatt, 2011) and during normal homeostasis (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012), we hypothesized that it does so by eliminating the competing survival signaling associated with cell-matrix attachment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Rosenblatt et al., 2001; Andrade and Rosenblatt, 2011; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012).

claim: Extrusion promotes cell death during normal homeostasis.
source: Because extrusion promotes cell death in response to apoptotic stimuli (Rosenblatt et al., 2001; Andrade and Rosenblatt, 2011) and during normal homeostasis (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012), we hypothesized that it does so by eliminating the competing survival signaling associated with cell-matrix attachment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012).

claim: Extrusion promotes cell death by eliminating the competing survival signaling associated with cell-matrix attachment.
source: Because extrusion promotes cell death in response to apoptotic stimuli (Rosenblatt et al., 2001; Andrade and Rosenblatt, 2011) and during normal homeostasis (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Marinari et al., 2012), we hypothesized that it does so by eliminating the competing survival signaling associated with cell-matrix attachment.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from prior work and the current study's findings.

claim: FAK is critical for matrix-dependent survival.
source: Since Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) is critical for matrix-dependent survival (Frisch et al., 1996), we investigated if FAK were increased in cells targeted for death when extrusion was blocked.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Frisch et al., 1996).

claim: S1P levels in cells triggered to extrude and die decrease once cells extrude.
source: This increase in pro-survival phospho-FAK in cells targeted to die mimics the increased levels of S1P, another pro-survival signal, in cells triggered to extrude and die that also decrease once cells extrude (Figure 3C and [Gu et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C and citation (Gu et al., 2011).

claim: Increased survival signaling in cells targeted to die may reflect cell-intrinsic compensatory signals to apoptotic signaling that eventually decrease as cells commit to apoptosis.
source: This paradoxical survival signaling increase in cells targeted to die may reflect cell-intrinsic compensatory signals to apoptotic signaling that eventually decrease as cells commit to apoptosis.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed data.

claim: Survival signals stay high when cell extrusion is blocked, suggesting that this increased survival signaling derives from inability to detach from matrix.
source: The fact that these survival signals stay high when cell extrusion is blocked suggests that this increased survival signaling derives from inability to detach from matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing persistent high phospho-FAK when extrusion is blocked.

claim: FAK inhibitor dramatically decreased phospho-FAK staining in cells where JTE013 blocks extrusion.
source: FAK inhibitor dramatically decreased phospho-FAK staining in cells where JTE013 blocks extrusion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.
